previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of morbid obesity, diabetes, chronic venous insufficiency, and heart failure was admitted after sustaining a traumatic wound to her right lower leg from a fall at her rehabilitation facility. The wound was deep, involving muscle and fascia, and she was admitted to vascular surgery for management. Her admission was complicated by acute kidney injury with elevated creatinine, likely due to dehydration, and a multidrug-resistant E. coli urinary tract infection sensitive only to meropenem. She was hydrated, her oral diabetes medications were held initially, and IV meropenem was started. After 24 hours of compression, she underwent debridement and VAC placement. Her kidney function improved, diabetes medications were resumed, and a PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic therapy. The wound developed healthy granulation tissue, and she was discharged to extended care with plans for readmission for skin grafting. She was stable, afebrile, and in good condition at discharge.

Brief Hospital Course:
Patient was admitted to the vascular service for plannd split 
thickness skin graft to cover an open non-healing RLE wound. She 
was consented and pre-oped and made NPO and was provided with IV 
fluids. She was also started on antibiotics for prophylactic 
coverage. She was taken to the OR on ___ for debridement of the 
wound and split thickness skin graft. A wound vac was placed in 
the OR and was set to 75mmHg negative pressure.  She tolerated 
the procedure well and was transferred back to the floor after a 
brief stay in the PACU. She was made bed rest and had foley 
placed on ___ due to bed rest status and difficulty with 
mobility due to body habitus. Her antibiotics was also 
discontinued. She tolerated a regular diet without difficulty.  
The rest of her recovery was uneventful with the exception of 
one bout of L thorax pain without radiation or shortness of 
breath. EKG was unchanged from pre-op, CK-MB and Troponin were 
within normal limits. Pain spontaneously resolved by noon.  Her 
creatinine increased from 1.3 to 1.6 on POD#3, however, her UOP 
remained in the >50cc/hour range. We did not bolus her due to 
her cardiac history.  Creatinine spontaneously returned to base 
line by ___. On ___ POD#6, wound vac was taken down, revealing 
intact graft site. She was made activity as tolerated, had her 
foley DC'd and worked with physical therapy. 

At time of discharge, she was in good pain control, afebrile, 
hemodynamically and neurologically stable.

Division of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery Discharge 
Instructions
 
What to expect when you go home:

1. It is normal to feel tired, this will last for ___ weeks 

·You should get up out of bed every day and gradually increase 
your activity each day 

·Increase your activities as you can tolerate- do not do too 
much right away!

2. It is normal to have swelling of the leg you were operated 
on:

·Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your 
legs elevated

3. It is normal to have a decreased appetite, your appetite will 
return with time 

·You will probably lose your taste for food and lose some weight 


·Eat small frequent meals

·It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber, 
lean meats, vegetables/fruits, low fat, low cholesterol) to 
maintain your strength and assist in wound healing

·To avoid constipation: eat a high fiber diet and use stool 
softener while taking pain medication

What activities you can and cannot do:

·No driving until post-op visit and you are no longer taking 
pain medications

·You may shower (unless you have stitches or foot incisions) no 
direct spray on incision, let the soapy water run over incision, 
rinse and pat dry. Cover the graft sites with tagederms when 
showering for the next week. Do not directly clean the graft 
site in the shower. 

·Take all the medications you were taking before surgery, unless 
otherwise directed

·Call and schedule an appointment to be seen in 2 weeks for 
staple/suture removal

What to report to office:

·Redness that extends away from your incision

·A sudden increase in pain that is not controlled with pain 
medication

·A sudden change in the ability to move or use your leg or the 
ability to feel your leg

·Temperature greater than 100.5F for 24 hours

·Bleeding, new or increased drainage from incision or white, 
yellow or green drainage from graft site and donor site.
